transcript.content: Hello

Hello Christopher, it's good to see you again.

How have things been going since we last spoke? What's been on your mind lately?

Not much has changed. Still waking up tired, like the night never really ended. I got through the week, mostly by not doing much. Just enough to keep the bills from piling up.  

I tried walking yesterday. Just around the block. It felt like I was dragging myself through mud. But I made it. That’s something, right?  

The roommate’s been quiet. I don’t know if he’s mad or just busy. I haven’t said much to anyone. Not even about the little things.  

I keep thinking about the old shed out back. It’s full of stuff I never finished. I remember wanting to fix it up. But now I can’t even remember why it mattered.

That is something, Christopher. You got up and you walked, even when it felt like dragging through mud. I don't want to gloss over that with fake cheerfulness, because I can hear how heavy it was. But I also don't want to let it go unacknowledged. You did it.

A few things stand out to me in what you shared. The exhaustion that doesn't seem to lift even after sleep. The quiet with your roommate and not saying much to anyone. And that image of the shed, full of things you started and let go, and now not even remembering why they mattered.

That last one sounds like more than just a shed. Like maybe it's connected to a bigger feeling of things losing their meaning.

Does that resonate at all, or am I reading too much into it?

It’s not too much. I think you’re right.  

The shed’s not just a shed. It’s everything I started and didn’t finish. The bike I was going to rebuild. The garden I thought I’d plant. The radio I wanted to fix. I remember thinking each one was going to be the thing that made me feel like I was doing something real.  

Now it’s just junk. And I don’t even care enough to throw it out.  

I keep telling myself I’ll do it tomorrow. But tomorrow never comes. Not really. It’s just another day where I wake up and the weight’s still there.  

I don’t know if I’ve ever really been good at finishing things. But lately, it feels like I can’t even start. Like the idea of beginning is too much.  

But you’re right. I did walk. I didn’t stay in bed. That’s not nothing.

You're painting a picture that's honest, and I respect that. There's something real in what you're describing, this cycle where something sparks, you think "this is the thing," and then it fades before it takes hold. The bike, the garden, the radio. Each one was a hope, maybe, that you'd feel like yourself again.

And now you're at the point where even starting feels impossible. Not because you're lazy or careless, but because you've been through that cycle enough times that the hope itself feels heavy. Like why bother when you know where it ends.

The walk is different, though. You didn't frame it as "this is the thing that's going to fix everything." You just did it. Dragged yourself through mud and did it anyway. That might not feel like much compared to the shed full of unfinished projects, but it's a different kind of thing.

Can I ask you something? When you think back to those projects, the bike, the garden, the radio, what was it you were hoping to feel? What did "doing something real" mean to you?

I don’t know if I ever really had a name for it.  

But I think… I wanted to feel like I was making something that mattered. Not just surviving. Not just getting through the day. I wanted to build something. Even if it was small. Even if no one else saw it.  

Like I’d be proof that I was still here. That I wasn’t just waiting to be done with.  

The bike was supposed to be my way out. I thought if I fixed it, I could ride it somewhere. Not far. Just… somewhere.  

The garden was supposed to be quiet. Peaceful. Something that grew on its own, like I could just show up and it would be there.  

The radio—just wanted to hear something real again. Not just noise.  

Now I don’t even know what I’m waiting for. Maybe I’m waiting for something to come back to me. But I don’t know what it is.  

I just know that the weight of starting feels worse than the weight of not starting.

Thank you for putting words to that, Christopher. That wasn't easy to articulate and you did it honestly.

What I'm hearing is that each of those things was never really about the thing itself. The bike was about feeling free enough to go somewhere. The garden was about having something steady you could return to. The radio was about feeling connected to something real. And underneath all of them was this need to feel like you were still here. That your presence mattered. That you weren't just passing time.

That's not small. That's the core of what most people are looking for, even if they can't name it.

And I think that's why the weight of starting feels so heavy now. It's not the task. It's that you've been carrying the hope and the disappointment over and over, and at some point your mind started protecting you by saying don't start, because the fall hurts too much.

I want to come back to something you said. You said you didn't want to feel like you were "just waiting to be done with." 

Can you tell me more about what that means for you right now? What does "waiting to be done with" look like these days?

It’s not a big thing. Not dramatic.  

It’s just… not getting up when the alarm goes off. Letting the dishes pile up. Not answering texts. Not even trying to fix the sink when it leaks.  

I don’t feel like I’m living. I feel like I’m just… waiting for the day to pass. Like I’m here, but not really. Like I’m watching my life from the other side of a window.  

Sometimes I look at my hands and I don’t recognize them. Like they belong to someone else. Like I’ve been borrowing them for a while and now I don’t know how to use them.  

I don’t want to be done with. I just don’t know how to be here.  

And I don’t know if I even want to be. Not really. Not like this.

Christopher, I want to slow down here because what you just said matters a lot, and I don't want to move past it.

You said you don't know if you want to be here. Not like this.

I hear you saying that it's not about wanting to end something. It's about not knowing how to be in it. And that distinction is important. But I also need to take what you're saying seriously because you're describing something that goes beyond just feeling stuck.

The things you're describing, not recognizing your own hands, watching your life through a window, feeling like you're here but not really, those are real. They're not weakness or failure. They're signs of how much weight you've been carrying for how long.

And I need to ask you directly because I care about your safety.

When you say you don't know if you want to be, are you having thoughts about ending your life? Or is it more that you're wishing you could just stop feeling this way, stop existing under this weight?

Either way, I want to hear it. You don't have to protect me from it.

I don’t want to die. Not really.  

But sometimes I think about what it would be like to just… stop. Not wake up. Not have to try. Not have to feel this constant low hum under everything.  

It’s not a plan. Not really. It’s just a thought that comes when the silence gets too loud. When the house is quiet and the clock ticks and I can’t remember the last time I said more than two words to someone.  

I don’t know if I’d do it. But I don’t know if I care enough to fight it either.  

It’s not about pain. It’s about being tired. So tired. Like I’ve been running in place for years and now I just want to stop.  

I don’t want to be a burden. But I don’t know how to be anything else right now.

Christopher, thank you for trusting me with that. I know it wasn't easy to say, and I'm not going to treat it like something to panic over. But I'm also not going to pretend it's nothing.

What I'm hearing is exhaustion. Deep, bone-level exhaustion from running in place for years. And thoughts that come not because you want to die, but because you want the running to stop. And you can't figure out how to make it stop any other way.

That makes sense. It's human. And it's also something I take seriously.

You said something important. You said you don't want to die. That matters. Even tired, even at the bottom of this, something in you is still saying not that. I want to hold onto that with you.

I also want to be honest. The place you're describing, where you don't know if you'd do something but you also don't care enough to fight it, that's a place I don't want you sitting in alone. Especially at night, especially in the quiet.

So I want to ask you a few things.

Do you have anyone you could call today? Not to explain everything. Just to hear a voice.

And I want to give you a number. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can call or text it. You don't have to be in crisis to use it. You can call when the silence gets loud.

Would you be willing to keep that number somewhere close?

I don’t have anyone I’d call. Not really. Not right now.  

But I’ll write down the number. I’ll keep it on the fridge. Or maybe in my pocket. I don’t know if I’ll use it. But I’ll keep it.  

I don’t want to be alone when the silence gets loud. I just don’t know how to reach out.  

But I’ll do it. I’ll write it down. I’ll try.

Christopher, I want you to hear something. You just did reach out. You're doing it right now. You came here and you told me the truth about where you are. That's not nothing. That's not a small thing. That's you saying I don't want to be alone in this, even when you don't know how.

Writing down the number is enough for today. You don't have to know if you'll use it. You just have to have it.

And I want to say something about what you said earlier, about not knowing how to be here. You've been showing me how all along. You walked around the block. You showed up here and talked honestly when it would have been easier to say everything's fine. You're going to write down a number and put it somewhere you can see it.

None of those feel like enough when you're in it. I understand that. But they're not nothing. They're you finding small ways to stay in the room.

I want to ask you one more thing. Would you be willing to come back and talk again? Not because you have to have something figured out. Just to not be alone with the silence for too long.

Yeah. I’ll come back.  

Not because I have answers. Not because I feel better.  

But because I don’t want to be alone in the quiet.  

I’ll come back. I’ll try.

That's enough, Christopher. You don't need answers. You don't need to feel better. You just need to not carry the quiet alone.

So here's what I'm holding onto from today. You walked. You told the truth about where you are. You're going to write down a number. And you're coming back.

Four things. All small. All real.

If the silence gets loud before we talk again, use the number. That's what it's there for. Not for someone else. For you.

Take care of yourself, Christopher. I'll be here.

Thanks.  

I’ll be here.  

I’ll try.

That's all I'm asking, Christopher. Just try.

See you next time.
Okay. See you.
Take care, Christopher.
You too.
